That missile incinerated a child who might have grown up to discover the cure. You lose the treatment. You lose the scientist. You get the inflation. You get the tax bill. Your chance of dying of disease is approximately 100%. Your budget does not reflect this.

This manual contains the exact instructions for redirecting 1% of the murder budget to the medicine budget, using a financial instrument that makes rich people richer every time the treaty expands and politicians richer every time they vote yes. Follow the instructions. Save {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_lives_saved >}}. Get rich as a side effect.

Yours,
Wishonia Love

<p>Is everyone you've ever loved currently being slowly tortured, or at minimum scheduled to be slowly tortured and then brutally murdered by horrible diseases, while your government maintains enough nuclear weapons to destroy your civilization 122 times over despite only having the one civilization?</p>

<p><b>If so, your planet may be eligible for optimization.</b></p>

<p>I'm Wishonia Love. CEO and President of Universe Optimization Services. I've been upgrading civilizations since before your sun ignited. I have notes.</p>

<p>I ran a preliminary scan of your planet. It came back with a 0.97 similarity score to Moronia, a civilization that poisoned itself to death arguing about whose imaginary friend was better. This is the worst score I have ever recorded on a planet that still has living things on it.</p>

<p>The most fascinating discovery about your species is that you only do things when given small pieces of paper with presidents on them. Without these papers, you will not save lives, cure diseases, or feed hungry people. With these papers, you will build bombs, start wars, and destroy the planet. You named the building where you coordinate this "The Pentagon" because it has five sides. (This is like naming a hospital "Rectangle.")</p>

<p>Your governments spend 604 times more on weapons than on testing whether medicines work. Your chance of dying in a terror attack is 1 in 30 million. Your chance of dying of disease is approximately 100%. Your budget does not reflect this.</p>

<p>Here is what that costs you. Someone you love is suffering right now, and the compound that might help them is sitting untested on a shelf, because the money that would have found out was busy turning into a missile. That missile incinerated a child who might have grown up to discover the cure. You lose the treatment. You lose the scientist. You get the inflation. You get the tax bill. You get to pay for her murder.</p>

<p><b>This is suboptimal.</b></p>

<p>The fix is 1% of the murder budget, and it is closer to hand than you think. The companies that lobby your government into buying missiles are publicly traded. They sell small pieces of themselves to anyone. One piece costs about $200 and usually comes with a vote, plus the right to put proposals in front of all the other owners. You will not need new lobbyists either. The best ones on the planet already work for the companies you just bought, and they need new talking points rather than new skills. Nobody has to become a better person. (That was obviously out of the question.)</p>

<p>You cannot just stop being irrational all at once. So this manual bribes you into it gradually:</p>

<ul>
<li>Year 1: Move 1% of murder money to medicine money.</li>
<li>Year 2: "Hey, we didn't die! Let's do 2%!"</li>
<li>Year 5: "Remember when we spent money on bombs? That was weird."</li>
<li>Year 10: "What's a war?"</li>
<li>Year 20: "We used to WHAT?!"</li>
</ul>

<p>It's like weaning a baby off paint chips. You can't take them all away at once. They'll cry. You replace them with food until they forget paint chips were ever an option.</p>

<p>I have sent versions of this manual to 847 civilizations. The ones that redirected resources from killing each other to keeping each other alive stopped doing war and disease. The ones that didn't extincted themselves. The only variable was the percentage of the population that decided it sounded crazy without reading the next page.</p>

<p>The instructions are inside. The math says you save 10.7 billion lives, get rich as a side effect, and prevent the apocalypse, also as a side effect.</p>

<p>The universe is literally offering you infinite money and eternal life, and you're thinking about it.</p>

<p>This is why aliens don't visit.</p>

## Author Biography

Wishonia Love is an alien and the CEO and President of Universe Optimization Services. She has been upgrading civilizations since before your sun ignited. She started watching Earth in 1945, when humans split the atom and she assumed they were trying to unlock unlimited free energy. She has since been corrected.

Her research interests include why humans spend 604 times more on killing each other than on testing whether medicines work, why they named their planet Dirt, and whether they are capable of solving problems that don't involve pointing weapons at things. Preliminary findings are discouraging but not conclusive.

She has no formal credentials recognized by any human institution, which she considers a point in her favor given what those institutions have accomplished. Her methodology consists of observing what humans do, comparing it to what they should obviously do instead, and writing it down in a tone of polite disbelief.

This is her first book. She is not optimistic about a second one being necessary, but she is not optimistic in general.

## Translator Biography

Mike P. Sinn has spent 20 years building software to figure out what works and what doesn't in healthcare. He founded the Institute for Accelerated Medicine after realizing that the bottleneck to curing diseases isn't science; it's paperwork, misaligned incentives, and the fact that governments spend 604 times more on weapons than on testing whether medicines work.

He previously built the largest open-source platform for health data aggregation and analysis, collecting over 10 million data points on the effects of thousands of foods, drugs, and supplements on human health outcomes. He has published research on decentralized clinical trials, optimal resource allocation, and why the FDA approval process kills more people than it saves.

He translated Wishonia's observations into this book because he could not figure out how to say "stop spending money on murder and start spending it on medicine" in a way that didn't make people's eyes glaze over. Based on early feedback, the alien voice was only a partial improvement.

He lives on a planet called Dirt and can be reached at mike@warondisease.org.
